topic.title: Why does Russia own a piece of land between Poland and Lithuania?
topic.map_answer: where Kaliningrad sits: the northern half of old East Prussia, given to the Soviet Union in 1945, left with Lithuania and Belarus between it and the rest of Russia when the Soviet Union's borders split in 1991

title: This piece of Russia doesn't touch Russia
description:
Kaliningrad is part of Russia, yet it sits alone on the Baltic between Poland and Lithuania. How did that happen?
One line across old East Prussia and one empire breaking up, told on the map, year by year.
Sources: City Population (Oct 2021). The characters are not advisers.
Maps simplified. Borders as recognised by the country each video is about.
cta: Stay Russian or join the neighbours: what would you choose? Comment

lines.text: This piece of Russia, on the Baltic, doesn't touch Russia at all.
It's Kaliningrad, squeezed between Poland and Lithuania. So how did Russia get here?
It covers 15,100 km² of forest, farms and long sandy beaches, about half the size of Belgium.
Turn the dial back a century, and this land was Germany: East Prussia, with its capital, Koenigsberg.
Then the Second World War ended, and the winners drew a line straight across East Prussia.
Poland got the south. The Soviet Union took the north, with its ice-free port.
Koenigsberg was renamed Kaliningrad, its Germans were sent west, and Soviet families moved in.
Back then, nobody minded: Lithuania, Latvia and Belarus were Soviet too, so the land ran unbroken to Moscow.
So what changed? In nineteen ninety-one, the Soviet Union fell apart.
Lithuania and Belarus became countries of their own, and overnight, Kaliningrad was stranded.
Now, to reach Moscow by land, a train from here crosses two other countries first.
Russia even keeps its Baltic Fleet there, in the port of Baltiysk.
And 1,029,966 people still live on this lonely piece of Russia, cut off from home.
Stay Russian, or join the neighbours: which would you pick? Because for now, this piece of Russia is on its own.

Re-review of the changed beats. hook: true, Kaliningrad has no land border with the rest of Russia. size: 15,100 km2 still confirmed (citypopulation.de oblast page; Britannica 15,100 sq km); forests, farms and the sandy beaches of the Curonian and Vistula spits are accurate, and half of Belgium holds. stranded: 'overnight' is rhetorical (Lithuania was recognised in Sept 1991, the USSR dissolved in Dec 1991) and acceptable as a style point. fleet (new): the Baltic Fleet is headquartered in Kaliningrad with its main base at Baltiysk (GlobalSecurity, FAS); a second base is at Kronstadt, so 'keeps its Baltic Fleet there' is broadly true. payoff: 1,029,966 at the 2021 census confirmed (2025 estimate 1,032,904). No advice, the tone is fine, and the description ends with the disclaimer.

Half of Belgium (30,689 km2) holds. History checked: East Prussia German in 1926, capital Koenigsberg; Potsdam 1945 split it, Poland south and USSR north; renamed 1946; Germans expelled by 1948 and Soviet settlers moved in; ice-free Baltic port; Lithuania, Latvia and Belarus Soviet until 1991. Moscow-Kaliningrad trains still cross Lithuania and Belarus (AFP Oct 2025, LRT Feb 2026). The topic has no verify list. No advice, tone is fine, and the description ends with the disclaimer.
